paragraphs.source_en: In addition to the resemblance in shape there are other important similarities between the Kel Essuf and Round Head anthropomorphic figures. In chapter 3 the most significant characteristic elements of the Round Head figures were presented and five of them are also associated with the Kel Essuf engravings, namely the half-moon objects attached on one or both shoulders (Fig. 4-4), the half-moon objects engraved singularly next to the figures and the figures with sticks and probable bows. In the Acacus and Djado the Kel Essuf engravings also present horns on the top of the head, the shape and position of which is similar to those on the Round Head figures. As mentioned in chapter 3, these characteristic elements never occur in the later Pastoral art or they do not occur in the same context, so that they must be considered particular for the cultural heritage of the local hunter-gatherers.

paragraphs.source_en: There is however one substantial difference between the Kel Essuf and Round Head anthropomorphic figures, namely the representation of probable penises. Almost every Kel Essuf image presents a third vertical line between the legs which is interpreted as a penis and this is confirmed by engravings in the Djado where this organ is also represented with the testicles (Hallier&Hallier 1999). Since other anatomical features on the Kel Essuf images are missing, the representation of the penis was apparently very important for some reason, perhaps as an indicator of the "maleness". This is a sharp contrast with the Round Head males who are never represented with penises3, as if it was a sort of a taboo, as were the eyes, which were also never represented.
